%  PART A.  SETUP
% ===========================================================================

\begin{definition}[Model and differencing]\label{def:model}
The structural model is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:levels}
Y_{ij} \;=\; \vdagger(X_{ij}) \;+\; Z_{ij}'\theta_\dagger \;+\; \eta_i \;+\; U_{ij},
\qquad j\in\{1,2\},
\end{equation}
with $X_{ij}\in\mathcal X\subset\IR$ scalar and continuously distributed, $Z_{ij}\in\IR^{p}$,
$W_i\in\{0,1\}$, and $\eta_i$ an individual effect that may depend on $(X,Z,W)$. Differencing across
the two periods,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diffs}
% \Delta\vdagger_i was a DOUBLE SUBSCRIPT error: \vdagger expands to
% \varphi_{\dagger}, which already carries one.  Written out here; the reading is
% fixed by the convention on the next line.  See preamble.tex at \vdagger.
\Delta Y_i \;=\; \Delta\varphi_{\dagger i} \;+\; \Delta Z_i'\theta_\dagger \;+\; \Delta U_i,
\qquad \Delta\varphi_i:=\varphi(X_{i2})-\varphi(X_{i1}),
\end{equation}
and, for a trial pair $(\varphi,\theta)$, the residual at trial values is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trialres}
\Delta U_i(\theta,\varphi)\;:=\;\Delta Y_i-\Delta\varphi_i-\Delta Z_i'\theta ,
\qquad \Delta U_i \;=\; \Delta U_i(\theta_\dagger,\vdagger).
\end{equation}
The subscript $i$ is suppressed whenever a statement concerns the population distribution $P$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Spaces, and the domain of the operator]\label{def:spaces}
Let $\pi$ be the reference density on $\mathcal X$ of Assumption~C1, and set
\[
\mathcal V\;:=\;\Big\{\varphi\in L^{2}(\mathcal X,\pi):\ \textstyle\int_{\mathcal X}\varphi\,d\pi=0\Big\},
\qquad
L^{2}(\Pi)\;:=\;L^{2}\big(\IR\times\mathcal T,\ \Pi\big),
\]
with $\Pi$ as in Assumption~B1(iv). Inner products are
$\langle h,h'\rangle_{L^2(\pi)}=\int hh'\,\pi\,dx$ and
$\langle\Xi,\Xi'\rangle_{L^2(\Pi)}=\int\Xi\Xi'\,d\Pi$.
% EXTRACTED FROM THE STATEMENT OF def:spaces ON 2026-08-03, under the house rule
% (.claude/references/theorem-environment-style.md) that a definition carries
% CONSTRUCTION ONLY.  WHICH LETTERS ARE THE BOUND VARIABLES on each side, and what
% species each names: rem:spacesread(1).

% repointed in the same pass: assumptions_supp.tex / assumptions.tex (H1's
% pre-image), results_supp.tex / results.tex (the generic element of L^2(Pi)),
% proofs.tex (prp:tccrepair's Xi, Xi'), and notation_glossary.md's C72, C89, C93,
% Xi_* and h rows.
The period-difference
% ARCHAEOLOGY (moved out of compiled text, shortening pass 2026-08-01).
% A round-11 draft wrote the two pairings as <a,b>, with a the RESERVED degree of
% ill-posedness and b the weight anchor b_star -- glossary C72's species, in the
% one display that defines the pairing.
operator is
$\Delta:\mathcal V\to L^{2}(P)$, $\Delta h=h(X_2)-h(X_1)$. For an integrable random variable $g$ write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nudef}
\nu_g(x)\;:=\;E[g\mid X_2=x]\,f_{X_2}(x)\;-\;E[g\mid X_1=x]\,f_{X_1}(x),
\qquad
\nu\;:=\;\nu_{\Delta Z}\in\IR^{p} ,
\end{equation}
the latter understood coordinatewise.

\emph{Every operator in this paper has domain $\mathcal V$, with one declared exception named below}, and
the decomposition $L^{2}(\pi)=\mathcal V\oplus\{\text{constants}\}$ is orthogonal.
% WHY THAT DECOMPOSITION HOLDS, why the restriction costs nothing, and which objects

\emph{The exception is the second-order form operator $\mathcal B$ of \eqref{eq:Bpi}, which is read on
all of $L^{2}(\pi)$}. \emph{No other object in the paper leaves $\mathcal V$.}

%  THE OPERATOR EQUATION.  This is the object missing from the source draft at
%  `:120--122', where the sentence ends "Then we have that" and the display
%  never appears.  Everything in draft Section 2 after that point -- the
%  Frechet derivative at `:124--126', the completeness condition at

\begin{definition}[The operator equation]\label{def:operator}
Let $\Delta Y_\theta:=\Delta Y-\Delta Z'\theta$, so that $\Delta U(\theta,\varphi)=\Delta Y_\theta-\Delta\varphi$.
For $(\varphi,\theta)\in\mathcal V\times\IR^{p}$ define the \emph{Bierens moment family}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mdef}
\mathcal M(u,t;\varphi,\theta)
\;:=\;E\Big[\widetilde W\;\un\big\{\Delta Y_\theta-\Delta\varphi\le u\big\}\;w\big(t'\Phi(\Delta Z)\big)\Big],
\qquad (u,t)\in\IR\times\mathcal T,
\end{equation}
with $\widetilde W=W-\varrho(\Delta Z)$, and let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Tdef}
T:\ \mathcal V\times\IR^{p}\longrightarrow L^{2}(\Pi),
\qquad
T(\varphi,\theta)\;:=\;\big[(u,t)\mapsto\mathcal M(u,t;\varphi,\theta)\big].
\end{equation}
The \emph{operator equation of the model} is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:opeq}
T(\varphi,\theta)\;=\;0 \quad\text{in }L^{2}(\Pi).
\end{equation}
We abbreviate $\mathcal M(u,t):=\mathcal M(u,t;\vdagger,\theta_\dagger)$ and
$T(\varphi):=T(\varphi,\theta_\dagger)$ when no ambiguity arises.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Admissible sets]\label{def:admissible}
Restrictions (A) and (B) of plan \S2.1 are
\[
\text{(A)}\quad E\big[\widetilde W\,\varsigma(\Delta U)\;\big|\;\Delta Z\big]=0\ \ \text{a.s. for every bounded measurable }\varsigma,
\qquad
\text{(B)}\quad E\big[\Delta Z\,\Delta U\big]=0 .
\]
Define
\[
\mathcal I\;:=\;\Big\{(\varphi,\theta)\in\mathcal V\times\IR^{p}:\ \Delta Y-\Delta\varphi-\Delta Z'\theta\ \upmodels\ W\ \big|\ \Delta Z\Big\},
\qquad
\mathcal V_{CI}\;:=\;\big\{\varphi\in\mathcal V:\ (\varphi,0)\in\mathcal I\big\}.
\]
Conditional independence $\xi\upmodels W\mid\Delta Z$ is understood in the factorisation sense,
$P(\xi\in B,\,W=j\mid\Delta Z)=P(\xi\in B\mid\Delta Z)\,P(W=j\mid\Delta Z)$ a.s.\ for all Borel $B$ and
$j\in\{0,1\}$. This is equivalent to the conditional-expectation form when both $W$-cells are non-null
given $\Delta Z$, and it is the form that behaves correctly when $W$ is conditionally degenerate --- in
which case it holds automatically, a fact used in the proof of \cref{lem:bierens}.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[$T$ is well defined and bounded]\label{prp:wellposed}
The moment family \eqref{eq:Mdef} defines an element of $L^{2}(\Pi)$ at every trial pair.
Suppose B1(i), (ii) and (iv.c) hold. Then for every $(\varphi,\theta)\in\mathcal V\times\IR^{p}$ the function
$\mathcal M(\cdot,\cdot;\varphi,\theta)$ is Borel measurable and
\[
\big\|T(\varphi,\theta)\big\|_{L^{2}(\Pi)}\;\le\;c_\Pi\;<\;\infty ,
\]
with $c_\Pi$ from Assumption~B1(iv.c), so that $T$ maps $\mathcal V\times\IR^{p}$ into a
ball of $L^{2}(\Pi)$ of radius not depending on $(\varphi,\theta)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Fr\'echet derivative in $\varphi$, with a Lipschitz derivative map]\label{prp:frechet}
$T$ is Fr\'echet differentiable in $\varphi$ with a quadratic remainder, and the derivative map is
Lipschitz.
Suppose B1(i), (ii) and (iv.c), C1 and C2$'$(i) hold. Then, for every $\theta\in\IR^{p}$ and every
$\varphi\in\mathcal V$, the linear operator $\mathcal A_\varphi:\mathcal V\to L^{2}(\Pi)$ defined by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Adef}
\mathcal A_\varphi h(u,t)
\;=\;E\Big[\widetilde W\,w\big(t'\Phi(\Delta Z)\big)\,
f_{\Delta Y_\theta-\Delta\varphi\mid X_1,X_2,\Delta Z,W}(u)\;\big\{h(X_2)-h(X_1)\big\}\Big]
\end{equation}
is bounded, with $\|\mathcal A_\varphi\|\le2\,\bar c_\pi^{1/2}\|\bar f_0\|_\infty c_\Pi$, and:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{Fr\'echet differentiability with a quadratic remainder:} for all $h\in\mathcal V$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:frechetbound}
\big\|T(\varphi+h,\theta)-T(\varphi,\theta)-\mathcal A_\varphi h\big\|_{L^{2}(\Pi)}
\;\le\;C_{\!\mathcal A}\,\|h\|_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2},
\qquad C_{\!\mathcal A}:=2\,\bar c_\pi\,\|\bar f_1\|_\infty\,c_\Pi ;
\end{equation}
\item[(ii)] \emph{Lipschitz derivative map:} for all $h\in\mathcal V$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lipschitz}
\big\|\mathcal A_{\varphi+h}-\mathcal A_\varphi\big\|\;\le\;2\,C_{\!\mathcal A}\,\|h\|_{L^{2}(\pi)} .
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
At the truth we write $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}:=\mathcal A_{\vdagger}$ with $\theta=\theta_\dagger$,
in which case the conditional density in \eqref{eq:Adef} is $f_{\Delta U\mid X_1,X_2,\Delta Z,W}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Compactness]\label{prp:compact}
$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is Hilbert--Schmidt, hence compact.
Suppose B1(i), (ii) and (iv.c), C1 and C2$'$(i) hold. Then $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the integral
operator on $\mathcal V$ with kernel
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kernel}
\mathsf k(u,t;x)\;=\;\frac{\nu_{g_{u,t}}(x)}{\pi(x)},
\qquad
g_{u,t}\;:=\;\widetilde W\,w\big(t'\Phi(\Delta Z)\big)\,f_{\Delta U\mid X_1,X_2,\Delta Z,W}(u),
\end{equation}
and $\|\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le 2\,\bar c_\pi\,\|\bar f_0\|_\infty\,c_\Pi<\infty$.
Moreover $\mathsf k(u,t;\cdot)\in\mathcal V$ for every $(u,t)$, so $\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}$ maps
$L^{2}(\Pi)$ into $\mathcal V$; and $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ admits a singular system
$(\sigma_j;e_j,\tilde e_j)_{j\in\mathcal J}$, $\mathcal J\subseteq\IN$, with $\{e_j\}_{j\in\mathcal J}$
an orthonormal basis of $(\ker\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}})^{\perp}\cap\mathcal V$ and, when $\mathcal J$ is
infinite, $\sigma_j\downarrow0$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{remark}[$\nu$ versus $\nu/\pi$]\label{rem:nupi}
Suppose in addition A1b(iv) holds, so that $\nu=\nu_{\Delta Z}$ is well defined. Then
$\int_{\mathcal X}(\nu/\pi)\,\pi\,dx=\int_{\mathcal X}\nu\,dx=0$, whereas
$\int_{\mathcal X}\nu\,\pi\,dx=E[\Delta Z\{\pi(X_2)-\pi(X_1)\}]$, which does not vanish for a generic
reference density. Since $\mathcal R(\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}})\subseteq\mathcal V$ by
\cref{prp:compact} and $\mathcal V=\{\zeta:\int\zeta\,\pi\,dx=0\}$, the source condition A2 can only be
imposed on $\nu/\pi$, never on $\nu$.
\end{remark}

% ===========================================================================
%  PART B.  STEP 1 -- SHIFT INVARIANCE
% ===========================================================================

\begin{lemma}[L1: shift invariance]\label{lem:shiftinv}
Restriction (A) is invariant to the value of $\theta$, so it does not identify $\theta_\dagger$.
The set $\mathcal I$ of \cref{def:admissible} satisfies, with no assumption beyond that definition,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shiftinv}
\mathcal I\;=\;\mathcal V_{CI}\times\IR^{p};
\end{equation}
and if in addition A1 holds, then $\vdagger\in\mathcal V_{CI}$, so $(\vdagger,\theta)\in\mathcal I$ for
every $\theta\in\IR^{p}$.
\end{lemma}

% THE SPLIT IS DELIBERATE.  Round 2 stated the whole lemma under A1, but Steps
% 1-2 of the proof establish \eqref{eq:shiftinv} from def:admissible ALONE; A1
% enters only the final clause.  Advertising A1 for the equality made cor:opsol
% -- which uses the equality and does not assume A1 -- not strictly citable
% against this lemma, and forced it to spend two sentences explaining which half
% it was using.  The split removes that.

\begin{remark}[R1]\label{rem:R1}
Three things follow from \cref{lem:shiftinv}, and one does not.

\emph{(i) What it establishes.} Restriction (A) carries no first-order information about
$\theta_\dagger$: the set of pairs it admits is a product set, so no functional of the conditional law
of the residual given $(W,\Delta Z)$ can distinguish $\theta_\dagger$ from any other $\theta$.

\emph{(ii) What it does not establish.} It does not say that $\theta_\dagger$ is unidentified.
$\theta_\dagger$ is identified by (B) alone: under A1 and A1b(iv),
\[
\theta_\dagger\;=\;\big(E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']\big)^{-1}E\big[\Delta Z\,(\Delta Y-\Delta\vdagger)\big],
\]
the inverse existing by A1b(iv) and the expectations being finite by the moment clauses of that same
assumption. \emph{This route uses neither A2 nor the retired A3.} A3 asserted nonsingularity of
$J=E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']+E[\widetilde W\ell_\star\Delta Z']$ and was itself conditional on A2; routing
identification of $\theta_\dagger$ through it would make identification contingent on a source condition,
which it is not. By \cref{lem:momzero}\textup{(iv)} the second summand is zero under A1, so $J$ is
$E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']$ wherever it is defined, and A3 is retired at A3 as a consequence of
A1 and A1b(iv). \emph{What must not be routed through A2 is the existence of $\ell_\star$}, and the
display above needs none of it. Nor does \cref{lem:shiftinv} say that
(A) is useless. A Neyman correction is mean-zero at the truth \emph{by construction} --- that is what
makes it a correction rather than a new restriction --- so ``carries no information about $\theta$'' is a
property of every Riesz representer in the debiased-machine-learning construction
\citep{chernozhukov2018dml}, not a defect peculiar to this model.
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  Through dispatch 12 this passage also called J "the different
% matrix"; that half is withdrawn, the separation the paragraph makes being
% unaffected and in fact sharper.  An earlier version of the project inferred from
% lem:shiftinv that the conditional form of A1 forces a two-step plug-in with no
% root-n theorem; the inference does not follow and was withdrawn.

\emph{(iii) What it costs.} Over-identification. Under an \emph{unconditional} independence assumption
one would have $\Delta Y-\Delta\vdagger-\Delta Z'\theta\not\upmodels W$ for $\theta\ne\theta_\dagger$
whenever $\Delta Z\not\upmodels W$, so (A) would carry information about $\theta$ and deliver a testable
restriction. Under A1 as stated, $\theta_\dagger$ is \emph{exactly} identified by (B) and (A) is a pure
debiasing device: \emph{(A) yields no over-identifying restriction on $\theta$}, which is precisely what
\cref{lem:shiftinv} proves. It does not follow that (A) is untestable. Solvability of the operator
equation remains testable in the usual nonparametric-instrumental-variables sense --- $\mathcal V_{CI}=\emptyset$
is an observable event, witnessed for instance by $\Delta Y=W\chi+e$ with $\chi\ne0$ and $e\upmodels W$,
where no $\varphi$ makes the residual conditionally independent of $W$. The claim to make in the paper is
about $\theta$, not about (A).

\emph{(iv) A population consequence, and a conditional algorithmic one.} By \cref{cor:opsol} the
solution set of \eqref{eq:opeq} in $\varphi$ is $\mathcal V_{CI}$ at every $\theta$, so \emph{as a
population statement} the first stage may be posed at any fixed $\theta$, including $\theta=0$, that is,
on raw $\Delta Y$. Two qualifications are required before this says anything about the estimator. First,
``targets $\vdagger$'' needs $\mathcal V_{CI}=\{\vdagger\}$, i.e.\ A1b(iii); without it the first stage
targets a set. Second, consistency of the \emph{regularised sample} solve is not delivered by
\cref{cor:opsol}: it is delivered by \cref{prp:phirate}, whose hypotheses --- A7 in its amended form
\eqref{eq:a7amend}, the spectral source condition (P-a.3), and the bandwidth condition (P-f) --- are conditions on
$\hat T(\cdot,\theta)$ and $\hat{\mathcal A}$, not on $T$, and must hold at the running value of
$\theta$. \emph{No tangential cone condition is among them}: A6 is retired
(A6, \cref{prp:tccfails}). What is $\theta$-free is the population
solution set.
What is emphatically not $\theta$-free is the conditioning of the inverse problem: $\mathcal A_\varphi$
in \eqref{eq:Adef} evaluates the conditional density at a $\theta$-dependent point, so the singular
values, the degree of ill-posedness $a$ and the source index $\mu$ are all $\theta$-specific.
\end{remark}

%  PART C.  STEP 2 -- THE BIERENS EQUIVALENCE
% ===========================================================================

\begin{lemma}[Bierens core]\label{lem:bierenscore}
A bounded, one-to-one transform and the exponential weight convert a conditional moment restriction into
an unconditional family indexed by a set of positive Lebesgue measure.
Suppose B1(i)--(iii) hold, $V$ is a random vector in $\IR^{p}$, and $\varepsilon$ is a random variable
with $E|\varepsilon|<\infty$. Then
\[
E\big[\varepsilon\mid V\big]=0\ \text{a.s.}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
E\big[\varepsilon\,e^{t'\Phi(V)}\big]=0\ \ \text{for every }t\in\mathcal T .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[L-3: quantifier management in $u$]\label{lem:quantu}
A family of conditional restrictions indexed by a real number reduces to a countable family, with a
single exceptional null set.
Fix $(\varphi,\theta)\in\mathcal V\times\IR^{p}$. Then there is a version of the
conditional distribution functions
$F^{(\theta,\varphi)}_j(u\mid z):=P\big(\Delta U(\theta,\varphi)\le u\mid W=j,\Delta Z=z\big)$,
$j\in\{0,1\}$, that is a distribution function in $u$ for every $z$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:binaryquant}
E\big[\widetilde W\,\un\{\Delta U(\theta,\varphi)\le u\}\mid\Delta Z=z\big]
\;=\;\varrho(z)\big(1-\varrho(z)\big)\Big\{F^{(\theta,\varphi)}_1(u\mid z)-F^{(\theta,\varphi)}_0(u\mid z)\Big\}
\end{equation}
for every $u\in\IR$ and a.e.\ $z$. Consequently, if the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:binaryquant} vanishes
for every $u$ in a countable dense subset of $\IR$ and a.e.\ $z$, then it vanishes for every $u\in\IR$
and every $z$ outside a single null set not depending on $u$.
\end{lemma}

% A4(i) IS NOT A HYPOTHESIS HERE, and its removal is a cleanup-pass correction.
% \eqref{eq:binaryquant} holds for ANY version of the conditional distribution
% functions, including on the degenerate region D := {z : varrho(z)(1-varrho(z))
% = 0} where one of the two W-cells is null and F_j(.|z) is an arbitrary
% version: on D the prefactor varrho(1-varrho) is zero, so both sides vanish
% whatever version is used.  The extension step needs only the POINTWISE
% positivity varrho(z)(1-varrho(z)) > 0, which the proof states in exactly that
% form, and it draws no conclusion on D -- where none is needed, since W is
% conditionally degenerate there and lem:bierens handles it separately.

\begin{lemma}[Bierens equivalence for the panel restriction]\label{lem:bierens}
The $\Delta Z$-conditional restriction (A) is equivalent to the vanishing of the unconditional family
$\{\mathcal M(u,t)\}$, so no conditional distribution given $\Delta Z$ ever has to be estimated.
Suppose B1(i)--(iv) hold. Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $\Delta U\upmodels W\mid\Delta Z$;
\item[(b)] $E[\widetilde W\,\varsigma(\Delta U)\mid\Delta Z]=0$ a.s.\ for every bounded measurable $\varsigma$, that is, restriction \textup{(A)};
\item[(c)] $\mathcal M(u,t)=0$ for every $(u,t)\in\IR\times\mathcal T$;
\item[(d)] $T(\vdagger,\theta_\dagger)=0$ in $L^{2}(\Pi)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{corollary}[to \cref{lem:shiftinv} and \cref{lem:bierens}]\label{cor:opsol}
The operator equation has the same solution set in $\varphi$ at every $\theta$, and that set is
$\mathcal V_{CI}$.
Suppose B1(i)--(iv) hold. Then for every $\theta\in\IR^{p}$,
\[
\big\{\varphi\in\mathcal V:\ T(\varphi,\theta)=0\ \text{in }L^{2}(\Pi)\big\}\;=\;\mathcal V_{CI},
\]
and under A1b(iii) this set equals $\{\vdagger\}$.
\end{corollary}

% NEITHER A1 NOR A4(i) IS A HYPOTHESIS of lem:bierens or cor:opsol.
%
% A1 would make lem:bierens VACUOUS: A1's first clause IS statement (a), so
% under A1 all four of (a)-(d) are true and the printed equivalence asserts
% nothing.  What is proved is that (a) <=> (b) <=> (c) <=> (d) whether or not
% the exogeneity restriction happens to hold.
%
% A4(i) IS IDLE, and the round-2 defence of it was wrong.  It claimed that
% without overlap "the restriction is vacuous wherever varrho in {0,1}, and (c)
% would not recover (a) on that region".  But on that region W is almost surely
% CONSTANT given Delta Z = z, and a conditionally degenerate random variable is
% conditionally independent of everything -- so (a) holds automatically there
% and there is nothing to recover.  Off it, lem:quantu needs only pointwise
% positivity.  And Wtilde = 0 almost surely on the degenerate region, so
% \eqref{eq:binaryquant} is trivially true there.  The old argument conflated
% "the restriction has no bite there" with "the equivalence fails there".
%
% NOTE ALSO WHAT THIS BUYS, and it is worth a sentence in the paper: with A4(i)
% gone, lem:bierens requires NO MOMENT CONDITION on Delta Y, Delta U or
% Delta Z, and NO LEBESGUE DENSITY for Delta U or Delta Z.  That is exactly
% what boundedness of Phi purchases -- see B1(i) and rem:Tcond -- and it is
% currently invisible in the statement.

\begin{lemma}[L-2: density of the closed span]\label{lem:density}
The debiasing weights representable through the Bierens family are dense, so the choice of weighting
measure is immaterial on the $\theta$-side.
Suppose B1(i)--(iii) and (v) hold, and let
\[
\mathcal G\;:=\;\overline{\operatorname{span}}\Big\{(u,z)\mapsto\varsigma(u)\,w\big(t'\Phi(z)\big):\ \varsigma\in C_b(\IR),\ t\in\mathcal T\Big\}
\]
with closure taken in $L^{2}(P_{\Delta U,\Delta Z})$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\mathcal G=L^{2}(P_{\Delta U,\Delta Z})$;
\item[(ii)] the set
$\mathcal G_\gamma:=\big\{L:L(u,z)=\int_{\mathcal T}\lambda(u,t)w(t'\Phi(z))\,\gamma(dt),\ \gamma\text{ finite signed satisfying B1(v)},\ \lambda\text{ bounded}\big\}$
is dense in $L^{2}(P_{\Delta U,\Delta Z})$;
\item[(iii)] $\overline{\{L-E[L\mid\Delta Z]:L\in\mathcal G_\gamma\}}
=\{L\in L^{2}(P_{\Delta U,\Delta Z}):E[L\mid\Delta Z]=0\}$, the subspace of weights \emph{satisfying}
N1.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{remark}[Why the weight is the exponential, and what a general analytic weight would cost]\label{rem:swintercept}
B1(ii) fixes $w=\exp$, and the restriction is substantive rather than expositional.

\emph{The textbook condition is not enough.} Suppose $w$ were required only to be real-analytic and
non-polynomial, as in the usual statement of the device. Take $V=\pm1$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each,
let $\Phi$ be the maintained componentwise $\arctan$ --- an \emph{odd} function, so
$\Phi(-1)=-\Phi(1)$ --- and set $\varepsilon:=V$. Then $E|\varepsilon|<\infty$ and
$E[\varepsilon\mid V]=V\neq0$, yet for $w=\cos$ and \emph{every} $t$,
\[
E\big[\varepsilon\,\cos\big(t\Phi(V)\big)\big]
\;=\;\tfrac12\cos\big(t\,\Phi(1)\big)-\tfrac12\cos\big(-t\,\Phi(1)\big)\;=\;0 .
\]
B1(i)--(iii) hold and the converse direction of \cref{lem:bierenscore} fails. The mechanism is that an
odd $\Phi$ against an even $w$ exposes only the even part of the image measure, so Step 4 of the proof
recovers the even moments and no others. The failure is not confined to the abstract lemma: with
$\Delta Z$ scalar and two-valued at $\pm c$,
$\mathcal M(u,t)=\cos\big(t\,\Phi(c)\big)\,E[\widetilde W\un\{\Delta U\le u\}]$, so (c) of
\cref{lem:bierens} holds
whenever the \emph{unconditional} restriction does, while the $\Delta Z$-conditional restriction can fail
through opposite-signed violations that cancel across the two values of $\Delta Z$.

\emph{The correct general statement, and what it would cost.} The repair is not to strengthen $\Phi$ but
to add an intercept. Index the family by $(t_0,t)$ over a subset of $\IR^{1+p}$ of positive Lebesgue
measure and use $\{w(t_0+t'\Phi(z))\}$. For $w$ real-analytic and non-polynomial, each derivative
$w^{(k)}$ is analytic and not identically zero --- otherwise $w$ is a polynomial --- so its zero set is
discrete and hence countable; therefore all but countably many $c\in\IR$ satisfy $w^{(k)}(c)\neq0$ for
every $k\ge0$, and the argument runs at such a $c$. This is the Stinchcombe--White family and the result
is \citet[Thm.~3.1]{stinchcombewhite1998}; it is load-bearing here, not a ``see also''. Adopting it
would change the range space to $L^{2}(\IR\times\mathcal T^{+},\Pi)$ with
$\mathcal T^{+}\subseteq\IR^{1+p}$, and would require the envelope bookkeeping of B1(iv)--(v) to be redone
with $\bar w(t_0,t)=\sup_{|v|\le|t_0|+c_\Phi\|t\|_1}|w(v)|$ throughout \cref{prp:wellposed},
\cref{prp:frechet} and \cref{prp:compact}.

\emph{Why it is not adopted.} $w=\exp$ is the maintained choice of the estimator, it is what
\citet[Thm.~1]{bierens1990} characterises --- so that the citation is exact rather than approximate ---
and the additional generality is consumed nowhere in the programme. The general family is recorded here
so that the statement is on the record without the range space paying for it.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[On $\mathcal T$, on $\gamma$, and on what compactness is for]\label{rem:Tcond}
It is worth recording what the identification layer costs, because the statement of \cref{lem:bierens}
does not show it. \emph{The equivalence requires no moment condition whatsoever on $\Delta Y$, $\Delta U$
or $\Delta Z$, and no Lebesgue density for $\Delta U$ or $\Delta Z$.} $\Delta Z$ may be discrete,
$\Delta U$ may have atoms, and neither need have a finite mean. That is exactly what boundedness of
$\Phi$ in B1(i) purchases: it makes $\varepsilon\,w(t'\Phi(\Delta Z))$ integrable for the bounded
$\varepsilon=\widetilde W\un\{\Delta U\le u\}$ with no condition on the law of $\Delta Z$, and it makes
the image measure of \cref{lem:bierenscore} compactly supported, hence determined by its moments. The
smoothness and moment conditions of C1, C2$'$ and A1b(iv) enter only when the \emph{operator} is
differentiated or the \emph{parameter} is identified, never in the equivalence itself.

Compactness of $\mathcal T$ is \emph{sufficient but not necessary} and should not be assumed. What the
proofs use is B1(iv.c) and B1(v), which for $w=\exp$ read
$\Pi_u(\IR)\int e^{2c_\Phi\|t\|_1}\Pi_t(dt)<\infty$ and $\int e^{c_\Phi\|t\|_1}|\gamma|(dt)<\infty$; a
compact $\mathcal T$ carrying a finite $\Pi_t$ and a finite $\gamma$ satisfies both, but so do many
unbounded index sets. Plan \S18.3 introduced compactness in order to license differentiation under the
$t$-integral. That is a specific interchange with a specific dominating function, and B1(v) now supplies
it: differentiating $L(u,z)=\int_{\mathcal T}\lambda(u,t)w(t'\Phi(z))\gamma(dt)$ in $u$ under the integral
sign is licensed by the bound $|\partial_u\lambda(u,t)\,w(t'\Phi(z))|\le\Lambda_1(t)\bar w(t)$, valid for
all $(u,z)$, together with $\int_{\mathcal T}\Lambda_1\bar w\,d|\gamma|<\infty$.

Two clauses of B1(iv) are minimal and should not be strengthened back. Step 5 of the proof of
\cref{lem:bierens} consumes only (iv.a), full topological support of $\Pi_u$ --- which is what makes the
zero set of $\mathcal M(\cdot,t)$ dense in $\IR$ --- and (iv.b), non-mutual-singularity of
$\mathrm{Leb}|_{\mathcal T_0}$ and $\Pi_t|_{\mathcal T_0}$, which is exactly the statement that no
$\Pi_t$-null set can swallow $\mathcal T_0$. Neither absolute continuity nor equivalence is used in
either factor.

Two things about (iv.b) are worth stating precisely, because it is easy to describe it wrongly. First,
by the Lebesgue decomposition it is equivalent to $\Pi_t$ having a nonzero absolutely continuous part,
so it excludes \emph{every} Lebesgue-singular $\Pi_t$ and not merely the atomic ones: a Cantor measure is
non-atomic, has uncountable support, and is excluded. Second, it is sufficient and not necessary. What
the argument really needs is an analytic-uniqueness condition on $\operatorname{supp}\Pi_t$: by Step 2 of the
proof of \cref{lem:bierenscore}, $t\mapsto\mathcal M(u,t)$ is real-analytic on all of $\IR^{p}$, so it
suffices that its zero set cannot contain $\operatorname{supp}\Pi_t$ up to a $\Pi_t$-null set unless it
vanishes identically. When $p=1$ that holds for any $\Pi_t$ whose support has an accumulation point --- a
Cantor measure included, since a Cantor set is perfect --- and \cref{lem:bierens} survives such a
$\Pi_t$. When $p\ge2$ the requirement is that $\operatorname{supp}\Pi_t$ not lie inside a proper
real-analytic variety, which positive Lebesgue measure guarantees and which many Lebesgue-null sets also
satisfy, but which perfectness alone does not: a hyperplane is perfect and is the zero set of a
coordinate. (iv.b) is retained as the clean sufficient version.

What (iv.b) does exclude in every dimension is a finite grid. \emph{The growing-family condition B1(vi)
is \textbf{retired}}, because the clause describes an estimator this programme does not implement:
\cref{def:hatTexp} integrates against $\Pi_t$ over all of $\mathcal T$ and never over a finite subfamily.
\emph{Identification of $\vdagger$ here is A1b(iii), assumed outright.} The exclusion (iv.b) performs is
recorded here so that it remains visible to a reader who reinstates the growing-grid design.
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  B1(vi) was classed an identification assumption rather than an
% approximation device on exactly the finite-grid ground above; the retirement is
% not a reversal of that classification, and the struck clause is kept in the
% corrected register in assumptions.tex rather than deleted.

The correction measure plays two different roles on the two sides of the construction.
\emph{On the estimation side} the
statement stands as written: by \cref{lem:density} the estimator \emph{solves for} $L$ inside a dense
class rather than integrating a fixed weighting measure against a continuum, so no $t$-integral is ever
computed in forming $\hat L$, and no weighting measure has to be chosen. This is also the surviving
argument against a continuum-GMM formulation: that would require choosing a weighting measure on
$\mathcal T$ and regularising the inverse of its covariance operator. \emph{On the population side the
integral representation is not optional.} The representer selected by the adjoint equation is an element
of $L^{2}(\Pi)$, and what makes it evaluable at $(\Delta U,\Delta Z)$ is exactly the induction map
$\mathcal W$ of \cref{lem:adjoint}(ii), which is an integral against $\Pi_t$. The correction measure of
B1(v) is therefore not a free object \emph{on that side}: \cref{lem:adjoint}(ii) identifies it with
$\Pi_t$, and \emph{at $\gamma=\Pi_t$, and only there}, the first half of B1(v) is implied by B1(iv.c)
rather than assumed, since
$\int\bar w\,d\Pi_t\le(\Pi_t(\mathcal T)\int\bar w^{2}d\Pi_t)^{1/2}<\infty$ by the Cauchy--Schwarz
inequality. \emph{That implication must not be widened.}
\Cref{lem:density}(ii) quantifies over \emph{every} finite signed $\gamma$
satisfying B1(v), and its proof constructs an \emph{atomic} $\gamma\ne\Pi_t$ for which the first half is
verified directly; so the first half is live on the estimation side and is retained for that reason,
while the second half is live here, in this remark, and is declined by \cref{cor:elldiff} for the reason
recorded there. What reconciles the two sides is \cref{lem:adjoint}(ii)'s density claim: the sieve and
the Bierens family parameterise the same closure, so the estimator may search the larger class without
losing the population object.

Finally, \cref{lem:bierens} is stated at the equivalence, not at a strict inclusion. The claim that
$\mathcal R(\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}})$ strictly contains the range of the unconditional adjoint is
not proved here and is not claimed: with $W$ binary the two moment classes are not nested, since
$\{g:E[g\mid\Delta U,\Delta Z]=0\}=\{\widetilde W\ell(\Delta U,\Delta Z)\}$ is an equality of sets, and
the comparison across the two modelling assumptions is heuristic. The conditional route is defended on
economic grounds and on internal consistency with the maintained exogeneity assumption, not on a weaker
source condition.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Two features of the linearisation that the derivation must not absorb]\label{rem:draftrec}
\emph{(i) The operator's arguments.} In \eqref{eq:Mdef} the $(x_1,x_2)$-integration is an expectation,
the $W$-argument is removed by the contrast $\widetilde W$ --- legitimate because $W$ is binary --- and
the $z$-argument is removed by the Bierens index $t$. What is left is indexed by $(u,t)$ with $u$
scalar, which is why the existing Landweber--Fridman machinery carries over with an enlarged index set
and no new curse of dimensionality.

\emph{(ii) Conditional versus unconditional centring.} A raw contrast between the two $W$-cells,
unconditional in $Z$, is \emph{not} the conditional operator reweighted by the scalar
$\varrho(1-\varrho)$, and the two do not share a range or a kernel. \emph{The correct comparison is
between kernels.} Write
$f_j(u):=f_{\Delta U\mid X_1,X_2,\Delta Z,W}(u\mid\cdot,\cdot,\cdot,j)$, the same conditional density
that appears in \eqref{eq:kernel}, and $p_X:=P(W=1\mid X_1,X_2,\Delta Z)$. The kernel of
$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ in \eqref{eq:kernel} is built from
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kernelcompare}
E\big[\widetilde W\,f_{\Delta U\mid X_1,X_2,\Delta Z,W}(u)\,\big|\,X_1,X_2,\Delta Z\big]
\;=\;p_X\,(1-\varrho)\,f_1(u)\;-\;(1-p_X)\,\varrho\,f_0(u),
\end{equation}
whereas the unconditional operator is built from $f_1(u)-f_0(u)$ up to sign. The two coincide up to the
factor $\varrho(1-\varrho)$ if and only if $p_X=\varrho$, that is,
if and only if $W\upmodels(X_1,X_2)\mid\Delta Z$ --- which says that \emph{the instrument does not shift
the endogenous regressor given $\Delta Z$}. \emph{It must not be assumed, and no equality of ranges or of
kernels is claimed here.} The identity
$E[\widetilde W\,g(W)\mid\Delta Z]=\varrho(1-\varrho)\{g(1)-g(0)\}$, which is correct, holds at
$\sigma(\Delta Z)$ and does not extend to $\sigma(X_1,X_2,\Delta Z)$; see convention (P4b) and its scope
warning in \texttt{proofs.tex}. The weights $p_X(1-\varrho)$ and $(1-p_X)\varrho$ in \eqref{eq:kernelcompare} are
bounded for free, all four factors lying in $[0,1]$; what A4(i) delivers is invertibility of the
prefactor in the one place the prefactor actually appears, namely at $\sigma(\Delta Z)$ in
\cref{lem:quantu}. There is in any case no second operator to reconcile with:
$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ \emph{is} the operator governing $\hat\varphi$.

\emph{(iii) The adjoint, and the factor that must not be cancelled.} The adjoint itself is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adjointdisplay}
\big(\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}\ell\big)(x)\;=\;\int_{\IR\times\mathcal T}\mathsf k(u,t;x)\,\ell(u,t)\,\Pi(du,dt)
\;=\;\frac{\nu_{\widetilde W\,(\mathcal W\ell)}(x)}{\pi(x)}
\qquad\text{with }\mathsf k\text{ from \eqref{eq:kernel}},
\end{equation}
so that $\langle\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}h,\ell\rangle_{L^2(\Pi)}=\langle h,\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}\ell\rangle_{L^2(\pi)}$
holds by construction; this is \cref{lem:adjoint}. \emph{Two things about
\eqref{eq:adjointdisplay} are load-bearing.} First, in the \emph{pairing}
$\langle\mathcal A h,\ell\rangle$ the $L^2(\pi)$ inner product contributes a factor $\pi$ and the
adjoint's own formula contributes $\pi^{-1}$, and the two cancel; that is a trap, because a reader who
cancels them concludes that the $L^2(\pi)$ weighting is immaterial, when the surviving $\pi^{-1}$ in
\eqref{eq:adjointdisplay} is exactly why the source condition A2 is imposed on $\nu/\pi$ and not on
$\nu$. Second, both subscripts $(\theta,\varphi)$ of the density are substantive:
\cref{prp:frechet}(ii) shows the $\varphi$-dependence is real, the derivative map being Lipschitz in
$\varphi$ with a nonzero constant; and \cref{rem:R1}(iv) records that the operator's singular values,
degree of ill-posedness and source index are all $\theta$-specific, because \eqref{eq:Adef} evaluates
the conditional density at a $\theta$-dependent point. \emph{What is $\theta$-free is a different object
--- the solution set of \eqref{eq:opeq} in $\varphi$, by \cref{lem:shiftinv}. The operator is not
$\theta$-free; only its zero set is.}

\emph{(iv) Two symbols.} The kernel $\un(x\ge v)$ is the kernel of
$\mathcal D^{-1}$, the integration operator of the derivative parameterisation; with the analysis
conducted in levels it does not appear. The letter $\psi$ is reserved for the moment function, so a
generic element of the range space is written $\ell$. \emph{And the range measure may not be left
implicit}: without $\Pi$ there is nothing to fix the range space, and displays that differ in whether a
$W$-argument survives silently use different ones. Under \cref{def:operator} the contrast
$\widetilde W$ removes the $W$-argument once and for all and the range is $L^{2}(\Pi)$ throughout.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[L-1: the difference and sum functionals]\label{lem:nusigma}
The period-difference operator is bounded with kernel the constants, and the two functionals it generates
differ in exactly one respect: the difference functional integrates to zero and the sum functional does
not.
Suppose C1(ii) holds and let $g$ be a random variable with $E|g\,h(X_1)|<\infty$ and $E|g\,h(X_2)|<\infty$
for the $h$ named in each clause. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\|\Delta h\|_{L^{2}(P)}\le2\,\bar c_\pi^{1/2}\|h\|_{L^{2}(\pi)}$ for every
$h\in L^{2}(\mathcal X,\pi)$ --- \emph{the whole ambient space and not only $\mathcal V$} --- so
$\Delta$ extends from the domain \cref{def:spaces} gives it to a bounded operator
$L^{2}(\mathcal X,\pi)\to L^{2}(P)$ with the same norm bound. \emph{The quantifier is stated at
$L^{2}(\mathcal X,\pi)$ because that is what the proof establishes and because three later results
consume it there}: the proof of \textup{(i)} uses $(a-b)^{2}\le2a^{2}+2b^{2}$ and C1(ii) and \textbf{never}
$\int h\,d\pi=0$, and C1(ii) is also what makes $\Delta h$ well defined for a $\pi$-equivalence class, since
$f_{X_j}\le\bar c_\pi\pi$ makes $P_{X_j}\ll\pi$ for $j=1,2$. \Cref{lem:prelimtheta} Step~4,
\cref{lem:epterm} Step~3 and \cref{lem:sandwich} Steps~3 and~6$'$ all apply this bound at
$h_k=\hat\varphi^{(-k)}-\vdagger$, whose membership of $\mathcal V$ would otherwise need A1b(i);
\emph{the wider quantifier removes that need at all three at once}, which is strictly preferable to
adding A1b(i) to three hypothesis lists.
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  Rounds 1--13 stated clause (i) "for every h in V"; the cost was
% the three unlisted A1b(i) uses named above.  An earlier record proposed adding
% A1b(i) to the three lists instead.
Clause \textup{(ii)} is a different matter and genuinely needs $h\in\mathcal V$;
\item[(ii)] $\Delta h=0$ almost surely if and only if $h$ is almost surely constant, provided A1b(ii)
holds; consequently, under A1b(ii) alone, $\ker\Delta\cap\mathcal V=\{0\}$ --- \emph{the passage from
``constant'' to ``zero'' is $\int h\,d\pi=0$ for $h\in\mathcal V$, which is \cref{def:spaces} and not an
assumption; A1b(i) is not needed, since it asserts $\vdagger\in\mathcal V$ and $h$ here is generic;}
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  Rounds 1--7 cited A1b(i) at this clause.
\item[(iii)] $E[g\,\Delta h]=\int_{\mathcal X}\nu_g(x)\,h(x)\,dx=\langle\nu_g/\pi,\,h\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi)}$,
for each $h$ satisfying the integrability proviso above --- in particular for every $h\in\mathcal V$ and
for $h\equiv1$;
\item[(iv)] $\int_{\mathcal X}\nu_g\,dx=0$ and $\int_{\mathcal X}\sigma_g\,dx=2\,E[g]$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sigmadef}
\sigma_g(x)\;:=\;E[g\mid X_2=x]\,f_{X_2}(x)\;+\;E[g\mid X_1=x]\,f_{X_1}(x);
\end{equation}
\item[(v)] if in addition A1 holds and $g=\widetilde W\,\Xi(\Delta U,\Delta Z)$ for an integrable
$\Xi$, then $E[g]=0$, hence $\int_{\mathcal X}\sigma_g\,dx=0$ as well.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[L-4: interchange in the adjoint direction]\label{lem:adjfubini}
The $(u,t)$-integration defining the adjoint may be taken inside the expectation.
Suppose B1(i), (ii), (iv.c), C1(ii) and C2$'$(i) hold, and recall from \cref{def:model} that $P$ is a
probability measure, hence $\sigma$-finite. Then for every $\ell\in L^{2}(\Pi)$ and every
$h\in\mathcal V$ the function
$(u,t,\omega)\mapsto g_{u,t}(\omega)\,\Delta h(\omega)\,\ell(u,t)$ is $\Pi\otimes P$-integrable, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adjenv}
\int_{\IR\times\mathcal T}E\big[\big|g_{u,t}\,\Delta h\big|\big]\,|\ell(u,t)|\,\Pi(du,dt)
\;\le\;2\,\bar c_\pi^{1/2}\,\|\bar f_0\|_\infty\,c_\Pi\,\|h\|_{L^{2}(\pi)}\,\|\ell\|_{L^{2}(\Pi)}
\;<\;\infty,
\end{equation}
and consequently
$\int_{\IR\times\mathcal T}E[g_{u,t}\Delta h]\,\ell(u,t)\,\Pi(du,dt)
=E\big[\Delta h\int_{\IR\times\mathcal T}g_{u,t}\,\ell(u,t)\,\Pi(du,dt)\big]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[L-5: levels versus derivatives]\label{lem:levels}
The orthogonality condition and the source condition are the same in the two parameterisations; the
remainder bound and the rate condition are not, and levels is the weaker of the two.
\emph{``The source condition'' in that headline means \textbf{A2}, a plain range condition, and clause
\textup{(iii)} states exactly that. It does \textbf{not} mean the source condition \emph{at index
$\mu_{\text{\textup{H1}}}=s/(2a)$},
which is \textbf{not} parameterisation-invariant}: composing with $\mathcal D^{-1}_0$ raises the degree of
ill-posedness from $a$ to $a+1$ and lowers the index from $s/(2a)$ to $(s-1)/(2(a+1))$, a loss of
$\tfrac83$ units of $s$ uniformly in $a$. \Cref{rem:tccwhy}\textup{(4)} is where that computation is used
and is this lemma's principal consumer.
Suppose A0's declaration of $\mathcal X$ as a compact interval and C1(ii) hold, and let
$\mathcal D^{-1}_0:L^{2}(\pi)\to\mathcal V$ be integration from the left endpoint $\underline x$ of
$\mathcal X$ followed by centring in $L^{2}(\pi)$. \emph{A1b(i) is \textbf{not} a hypothesis here}: all
four clauses concern generic $h,h',\nu_g$, the codomain $\mathcal V$ is \cref{def:spaces}, and
$\vdagger$ does not occur in the statement or in any step of the proof. Then
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  A1b(i) was listed on this line through round 7 and is struck.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\mathcal D^{-1}_0$ is bounded, with
$\|\mathcal D^{-1}_0\|\le2\,(\,|\mathcal X|\,\|1/\pi\|_\infty)^{1/2}$, and injective, while
$\mathcal D$ is unbounded on $L^{2}(\pi)$;
\item[(ii)] for integrable $\nu_g$, writing $\mathcal N_g(v):=\int_{\{x\ge v\}\cap\mathcal X}\nu_g(x)\,dx$,
one has $\mathcal N_g\equiv0$ if and only if $\nu_g\equiv0$ almost everywhere on $\mathcal X$;
\item[(iii)] A2 holds for $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ if and only if the corresponding source condition
holds for $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}\mathcal D^{-1}_0$;
\item[(iv)] $\|h\|_{L^{2}(\pi)}\le\|\mathcal D^{-1}_0\|\,\|h'\|_{L^{2}(\pi)}$ whenever
$h=\mathcal D^{-1}_0h'$, so a rate in the derivative norm implies the same rate in the level norm, while
the converse fails.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Closed form of the adjoint]\label{lem:adjoint}
The adjoint of the linearisation is the difference functional of the debiasing weight, divided by the
reference density, once the weight is read through the Bierens family.
Suppose B1(i), (ii), (iv) hold together with C1(ii) and C2$'$(i). Then, with
$g_{u,t}$ as in \eqref{eq:kernel}:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{Kernel form.} For every $\ell\in L^{2}(\Pi)$,
$\big(\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}\ell\big)(x)=\int_{\IR\times\mathcal T}\mathsf k(u,t;x)\,\ell(u,t)\,\Pi(du,dt)$,
and $\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}\ell\in\mathcal V$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{The induction map.} The operator
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Wdef}
\big(\mathcal W\ell\big)(u,z)\;:=\;\varpi_u(u)\int_{\mathcal T}\ell(u,t)\,w\big(t'\Phi(z)\big)\,\Pi_t(dt),
\qquad (u,z)\in\IR\times\IR^{p},
\end{equation}
is a bounded linear map from $L^{2}(\Pi)$ into $L^{2}(P_{\Delta U,\Delta Z})$ with
$\|\mathcal W\|\le\big(\|\bar f_0\|_\infty\,\|\varpi_u\|_\infty\int_{\mathcal T}\bar w^{2}\,d\Pi_t\big)^{1/2}$,
its range is dense in $L^{2}(P_{\Delta U,\Delta Z})$, and
$\ker\mathcal W\subseteq\ker\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{Closed form.} For every $\ell\in L^{2}(\Pi)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adjclosed}
\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}\ell\;=\;\frac{\nu_{\widetilde W\,(\mathcal W\ell)}}{\pi} ,
\end{equation}
where $\widetilde W(\mathcal W\ell)$ abbreviates $\widetilde W\,(\mathcal W\ell)(\Delta U,\Delta Z)$;
consequently $\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}\ell=-\nu/\pi$ if and only if
$\nu_{\Delta Z+\widetilde W(\mathcal W\ell)}\equiv0$ almost everywhere on $\mathcal X$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{corollary}[to \cref{lem:adjoint}: the representer is differentiable, with explicit bounds]\label{cor:elldiff}
Regularity of a range-space representer transfers to its observable-space image, and the transfer
is what makes the sup-norm requirements of A2$'$ well posed.
\emph{Stated at a generic admissible representer, with $\ell^\Pi_\star$ as the specialisation.} Suppose
B1(i), (ii), (iv.a) hold and let $\ell^\Pi\in L^{2}(\Pi)$ be an \emph{admissible representer} in the
sense of A2b, with budgets $\Lambda^{(0)},\Lambda^{(1)}$ and with $\ell:=\mathcal W\ell^\Pi$ defined
pointwise from the version A2b fixes. Then $\ell$ is bounded, is continuously differentiable in $u$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Wderiv}
\partial_u\ell(u,z)
=\varpi_u'(u)\!\int_{\mathcal T}\!\ell^\Pi(u,t)\,w(t'\Phi(z))\,\Pi_t(dt)
+\varpi_u(u)\!\int_{\mathcal T}\!\partial_u\ell^\Pi(u,t)\,w(t'\Phi(z))\,\Pi_t(dt),
\end{equation}
and satisfies
\[
\big\|\ell\big\|_\infty\le\|\varpi_u\|_\infty\,\Lambda^{(0)},
\qquad
\big\|\partial_u\ell\big\|_\infty\le\|\varpi_u'\|_\infty\,\Lambda^{(0)}+\|\varpi_u\|_\infty\,\Lambda^{(1)} .
\]
\emph{Specialisation.} Under A2$'$(i.a)--(i.b) the selected solution $\ell^\Pi_\star$ is an admissible
representer with $\Lambda^{(0)}=\Lambda^{(0)}_\star$, $\Lambda^{(1)}=\Lambda^{(1)}_\star$, so the
corollary applies at $\ell=\ell_\star:=\mathcal W\ell^\Pi_\star$ and yields
$\|\ell_\star\|_\infty\le\|\varpi_u\|_\infty\Lambda^{(0)}_\star$ and
$\|\partial_u\ell_\star\|_\infty\le\|\varpi_u'\|_\infty\Lambda^{(0)}_\star+\|\varpi_u\|_\infty\Lambda^{(1)}_\star$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[to \cref{lem:adjoint}: how far A2 can exceed what the moment needs]\label{cor:rangegap}
The source condition and the orthogonality equation the estimator targets can differ only inside the
non-closedness of the range of the adjoint.
Suppose the hypotheses of \cref{lem:adjoint} hold together with A1b(iv), and define the
\emph{tilted difference map}
$\Upsilon:L^{2}(P_{\Delta U,\Delta Z})\to\mathcal V$ by
$\Upsilon\Xi:=\nu_{\widetilde W\Xi}/\pi$. Then $\Upsilon$ is a bounded linear operator with
$\|\Upsilon\|\le2\,\bar c_\pi^{1/2}$, $\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}=\Upsilon\circ\mathcal W$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rangegap}
\mathcal R\big(\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}\big)\;\subseteq\;\mathcal R(\Upsilon)\;\subseteq\;
\overline{\mathcal R\big(\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}\big)} .
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Consequences of \cref{lem:adjoint}, and one independent confirmation]\label{rem:adjointreconcile}
Four things follow, three of which later results consume.

\emph{(i) The representer is evaluable at the data, and that is now a theorem.} A solution of the adjoint
equation is an element of $L^{2}(\Pi)$, a function of $(u,t)$ with $t$ the Bierens index, while
A2$'$(i), whose closing sentence fixes $\ell_\star:=\mathcal W\ell^\Pi_\star$ pointwise, and
\eqref{eq:JSig} evaluate $\ell_\star(\Delta U,\Delta Z)$ with $z$ a value of $\Delta Z$. Part (ii)
supplies the map between the two and part (iii) shows it commutes with the adjoint equation, so the object
A2$'$(i) and \eqref{eq:JSig} speak about is constructed rather than posited. \emph{And \eqref{eq:Wdef} is
exactly why the evaluation is well posed}: $\ell_\star=\mathcal W\ell^\Pi_\star$ is a Borel map of
$(u,z)$ and of nothing else --- in particular not of $W$ --- which is the measurability
\cref{lem:momzero}\textup{(iv)} consumes. \emph{The construction consumes exactly one thing beyond the
identification block}: absolute continuity of $\Pi_u$ in B1(iv.a), a restriction on a reference
measure the analyst chooses.
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  Through dispatch 13 the first citation on this item read
% "A2'(i)--(ii)"; A2'(ii) is retired and the clause that evaluates ell_star at the
% data was always (i).  Through dispatch 12 the second citation read "A3"; that tag
% is retired at ass:rank and the display it presupposed is eq:JSig.

\emph{(ii) The correction measure is not free \textup{on the population side}}, the map \eqref{eq:Wdef}
integrating against $\Pi_t$; \cref{rem:Tcond} carries the disposition of B1(v)'s two halves.

\emph{(iii) What the construction does not give, and what it gives anyway.} $\mathcal W$ has dense range
but need not be surjective, so a selection criterion posed over all of $L^{2}(P_{\Delta U,\Delta Z})$ may
be unreachable; and $\mathcal W$ need not be injective, though
$\ker\mathcal W\subseteq\ker\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}$ means no direction relevant to the selection
is lost. \emph{It does not follow that the gap between A2 and the equation the estimator targets is
uncontrolled.} By \cref{cor:rangegap}, $\mathcal R(\Upsilon)$ --- the set of $\nu/\pi$ for which the
primitive orthogonality equation is solvable in $L^{2}(P_{\Delta U,\Delta Z})$ --- is squeezed between
$\mathcal R(\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}})$ and its closure, \emph{with no characterisation of
$\mathcal R(\mathcal W)$ required}. So A2 can exceed what the moment needs only within
$\overline{\mathcal R(\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}})}\setminus\mathcal R(\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}})$.
That set is nonempty under H1: $\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is compact, being the adjoint of a
compact operator, and a compact operator has closed range if and only if that range is
finite-dimensional, which H1's infinite-rank clause excludes. \emph{Injectivity is neither available nor
needed for this} --- $\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}$ may well have a kernel, since
$\ker\mathcal W\subseteq\ker\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}$ two sentences above. The
gap is therefore exactly where the ill-posedness lives.
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  An earlier version of this item gave injectivity of A*_cond as the
% reason the gap is nonempty; it was both unavailable and superfluous.

\emph{(iv$'$) The derivative of the representer.} The sup-norm requirements on $\ell_\star$ remain
assumptions, but they are stated on $\ell^\Pi_\star$, in A2$'$(i.a)--(i.b), and
\cref{cor:elldiff} derives from them both \eqref{eq:Wderiv} and the two bounds. \emph{The ordering
matters}: the $C^{1}$ clause of B1(iv.a) alone controls only the first term of
\eqref{eq:Wderiv}, so $\|\partial_u\ell_\star\|_\infty<\infty$ cannot be assumed directly without
assuming the existence of a derivative nothing else in the block delivers.
\eqref{eq:Wderiv} is what makes the choice of $\Pi_u$ a design lever on $q$ and on
$\sigma_q$; it is a \emph{conditional} identity whose hypothesis is A2$'$(i.b), and A2$'$(i.b) is a
primitive awaiting L-21, not a theorem.

\emph{(iv) The $\nu/\pi$ referent is confirmed independently, and in the same form.} \emph{Notation:}
\citet{feve2014} write the endogenous regressors as $Z_1,Z_2$ with generic value $z$, the instrument as
$W$ with generic value $w$, and a generic element of the range space as $\psi$; the translation to this
paper is $Z_t\mapsto X_t$, $z\mapsto x$, and their $\psi$ is our $\ell$, the letter $\psi$ being reserved
here for the moment function. For the linear conditional-mean panel operator
$K\varphi=E[\varphi(Z_2)-\varphi(Z_1)\mid W]$, their Proposition~2.1 gives, \emph{verbatim in their
notation},
\[
\big(K^{\ast}\psi\big)(z)\;=\;\int\psi(w)\,\frac{f_{Z_2,W}(z,w)-f_{Z_1,W}(z,w)}{\pi(z)}\,dw ,
\]
followed immediately by the statement that $K^{\ast}\psi$ satisfies the normalising constraint
$\int\big[(K^{\ast}\psi)(z)\big]\pi(z)\,dz=0$. Translated, the numerator is $\nu_{\ell(W)}$ and the
display is $\nu_{\ell(W)}/\pi$. \emph{One difference of setting must be flagged rather than absorbed:}
their $dw$ integral ranges over a general instrument space, whereas $W$ is binary here, so the
counterpart in this paper is the two-point sum
$\nu_{\ell(W)}(x)=\sum_{j\in\{0,1\}}\ell(j)\{f_{X_2,W}(x,j)-f_{X_1,W}(x,j)\}$; the difference-of-densities
structure is what carries over, not the integral.

\emph{Both features of \eqref{eq:adjclosed} therefore appear in print in the linear case:} the division
by the reference density --- with the same letter $\pi$, which the draft takes from them --- and the zero
$\pi$-mean, which is membership of $\mathcal V$ and which \cref{prp:compact} Step~2 proves here from
$\int\nu_g\,dx=0$ at $h\equiv1$. This matters because the referent was contested: an earlier version of
this project imposed the source condition on $\nu$ rather than on $\nu/\pi$, and the correction was
forced internally by a Picard membership test. \emph{The $\pi^{-1}$ is not an artefact of the
$L^{2}(\pi)$ convention adopted here; it is the shape the adjoint takes in a first-differenced panel.}
What transfers is that shape and nothing more: their $K$ is a fixed linear conditional-expectation
operator, while $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is a Fr\'echet derivative, and the induction map
$\mathcal W$ in \eqref{eq:adjclosed} has no counterpart there because their restriction is already
unconditional in the residual.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[R2: when a weight yields a $\varphi$-free moment]\label{prp:nophifree}
A moment is free of the structural function exactly when the two periods' $g$-tilted marginals of the
endogenous regressor coincide.
Suppose C1(ii) holds and let $g$ be a random variable satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gproviso}
E|g|<\infty,
\qquad
E\big|g\,h(X_j)\big|<\infty\ \ (j=1,2)\ \text{for every }h\in\mathcal V,
\qquad
E\big|g\,\Delta U(\theta,0)\big|<\infty .
\end{equation}
Then the map $\varphi\mapsto E\big[g\,\Delta U(\theta,\varphi)\big]$ is constant on $\mathcal V$, for one
and hence every $\theta\in\IR^{p}$, if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tilted}
E[g\mid X_2=x]\,f_{X_2}(x)\;=\;E[g\mid X_1=x]\,f_{X_1}(x)
\qquad\text{for almost every }x\in\mathcal X,
\end{equation}
that is, if and only if $\nu_g\equiv0$.
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  A1b(i) was listed as a hypothesis here through round 7 and is
% struck.  Why it is not one: rem:nophifree(v).
\end{proposition}

\begin{corollary}[to \cref{prp:nophifree}: the debiasing weight must vary with the residual]\label{cor:udep}
If the debiasing weight does not depend on the residual, the debiased moment is not merely
first-order insensitive to the structural function but exactly free of it.
Suppose A1, A1b(i), A1b(iv) and C1(ii) hold, let $L$ be differentiable in $u$ \emph{at every} $(u,z)$
with $\partial_uL(u,z)=c(z)$ for some $c$ such that $g:=\Delta Z+\widetilde W\,c(\Delta Z)$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:gproviso} coordinatewise, and suppose $L$ satisfies N1. Then
$L(u,z)=c(z)\,u$, the moment function is $\psi=g\,\Delta U(\theta,\varphi)$ with $g$ measurable with
respect to $\sigma(W,\Delta Z)$, and the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $E[\psi]$ is first-order insensitive to $\varphi$ at $\vdagger$, i.e.\
$\nu_{\Delta Z+\widetilde Wc}\equiv0$;
\item[(b)] $\varphi\mapsto E[\psi]$ is constant on $\mathcal V$;
\item[(c)] $\nu_{\widetilde Wc}=-\nu$ \emph{for the $c$ of the hypothesis}; equivalently, membership
$-\nu\in\mathcal N_0:=\{\nu_{\widetilde W\,\tilde c(\Delta Z)}:\tilde c\in\mathcal C_0\}$ is realised
\emph{at that} $c$, where $\mathcal C_0$ is the set of $\tilde c$ for which
$\Delta Z+\widetilde W\tilde c(\Delta Z)$ satisfies \eqref{eq:gproviso} coordinatewise.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover $\varphi\mapsto E[\psi]$ is affine on $\mathcal V$, so every term of order two or higher in its
expansion vanishes identically \emph{whether or not \textup{(a)--(c)} hold}; what \textup{(a)--(c)} add is
that the first-order term vanishes as well. Contrapositively, if $-\nu\notin\mathcal N_0$, then every
$\ell_\star$ satisfying $\nu_{\Delta Z+\widetilde W\ell_\star}\equiv0$ has
$\partial_u\ell_\star\not\equiv0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[What the impossibility result says, and where it has been seen before]\label{rem:nophifree}
\Cref{prp:nophifree} is the paper's negative result, and three readings of \eqref{eq:tilted} are worth
separating.

\emph{(i) The condition, in words.} Write $\tilde f^{\,g}_j(x):=E[g\mid X_j=x]f_{X_j}(x)$ for the
$g$-tilted density of the endogenous regressor in period $j$ --- a signed density of total mass $E[g]$.
Condition \eqref{eq:tilted} says $\tilde f^{\,g}_1=\tilde f^{\,g}_2$: \emph{the two periods' $g$-tilted
marginals coincide.} At $g\equiv1$ this is marginal stationarity of $X$, so even the unweighted moment
$E[\Delta U]$ is free of $\varphi$ only when the regressor's marginal law does not move between the two
periods. At $g=\Delta Z_j$ it is $\nu\equiv0$, which is probe CP-1 and the design in which the debiasing
weight degenerates to zero and the moment reduces to the differenced least-squares one. The failure of
\eqref{eq:tilted} is therefore not a pathology to be assumed away: it is what makes the panel design
informative in the first place, and a design in which it holds for the weights of interest is one in
which there is nothing to debias.

\emph{(ii) The same condition, reached independently in the linear case.} In the first-differenced panel
with a conditional-mean restriction, \citet{feve2014} observe that the operator
$\varphi\mapsto E[\varphi(X_2)-\varphi(X_1)\mid W]$ annihilates \emph{every} $\varphi$ when
$(X_1,X_2,W)$ has the same law as $(X_2,X_1,W)$ --- exchangeability of the two periods given the
instrument, which in particular equates the laws of $(X_1,W)$ and $(X_2,W)$. That is \eqref{eq:tilted}
imposed simultaneously for every bounded $g=g(W)$, since
$\nu_{g(W)}(x)=\sum_{j\in\{0,1\}}g(j)\{f_{X_2,W}(x,j)-f_{X_1,W}(x,j)\}$. Their Proposition~2.1 gives the
adjoint of that operator as an integral against the same difference of joint densities over the same
reference density; see \cref{rem:adjointreconcile}(iv). \emph{The difference structure is therefore not a
device of this paper: it is inherited from first differencing and is shared with the linear
conditional-mean design.} What \cref{prp:nophifree} adds is the one-weight-at-a-time equivalence --- their
condition is the simultaneous one, and is correspondingly stronger --- and the enlargement of $g$ from
functions of $W$ to functions of $(W,\Delta Z)$, which is the class the debiasing construction actually
searches.

\emph{(iii) What is new here, stated precisely.} The sharp difference from \citet{feve2014} is not that
their operator is linear and ours is not, which is true but too coarse. It is that
$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is a \emph{Fr\'echet derivative of a nonlinear map} rather than a fixed
linear conditional-expectation operator, and three consequences follow that have no counterpart there:
the operator depends on the point of linearisation, with the Lipschitz modulus of
\cref{prp:frechet}(ii); the sample operator is noisy \emph{as an operator}, which is why the
regularisation conditions of this block --- A7, and the retired A6 before it --- are stated for
$\hat T$ and not for $T$; and the moment carries a second-order term in $\varphi$, which is
\cref{cor:udep}'s subject and which a linear operator equation does not produce.

\emph{(iv) Why the negative result creates the rate requirement, and what the chain does not contain.}
\Cref{cor:udep} closes the chain. If the debiasing weight ignored the residual, the moment would reduce
to a $\sigma(W,\Delta Z)$-measurable weight times the residual, and orthogonality would then force
\eqref{eq:tilted}; in any design where \eqref{eq:tilted} fails for such weights, the selected
$\ell_\star$ must vary with the residual. That is what puts $\partial_u\ell_\star$ into the second-order
term, and it is why a quadratic remainder in $\varphi$ is unavoidable within this moment class rather
than an artefact of the expansion. \emph{Two things are not in the chain and should not be read into it.}
First, $\partial_u\ell_\star\not\equiv0$ is \emph{necessary} for the second-order form to be nonzero and
not sufficient: the conditional expectation
$q(x_1,x_2)=E[\widetilde W\partial_u\ell_\star\mid X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2]$ could still vanish by cancellation,
and excluding that is a separate hypothesis. Second, \cref{prp:nophifree} is an equivalence, not an
impossibility theorem: it does not assert that \eqref{eq:tilted} fails. Whether it fails is a property of
the application, testable through the Picard diagnostic and through $\hat\nu_g$ directly, and the paper
should report it rather than assert it.

% EXTRACTED FROM THE STATEMENTS OF prp:nophifree AND cor:a1cprim on 2026-08-02.
% Both carried a "not a hypothesis" paragraph inside the printed statement; both
% paragraphs are about the hypothesis LIST and not about what is claimed.  The
% clause is struck from neither list -- it was never in either -- so nothing about
% either result changes.
\emph{(v) A1b(i) is \textbf{not} a hypothesis of \cref{prp:nophifree}, and it is not one of
\cref{cor:a1cprim} either.} For \cref{prp:nophifree}: the proof's third step upgrades
``$\nu_g/\pi\perp\mathcal V$'' to ``$\nu_g\equiv0$'' using
$L^{2}(\pi)=\mathcal V\oplus\{\text{constants}\}$ --- which is \cref{def:spaces} --- together with
$\int_{\mathcal X}\nu_g\,dx=0$ from \cref{lem:nusigma}(iv); $\vdagger$ occurs nowhere in the statement or
the proof, and the map is quantified over generic $\varphi,\varphi_0\in\mathcal V$. For
\cref{cor:a1cprim}: the ``constant, hence zero'' step of \cref{lem:nusigma}\textup{(ii)} is
\cref{def:spaces} and not that clause, and the conclusion is about a generic
$h\in\ker\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}\subseteq\mathcal V$.
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  A1b(i) was listed as a hypothesis of both through round 7, and is
% struck from both; cor:a1cprim inherited it from lem:nusigma(ii).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Characterisation of the kernel of the linearisation]\label{prp:kerchar}
A direction is annihilated by the linearised operator exactly when the instrument fails to move its
period difference, given the residual and the controls.
Suppose B1(i)--(iv), C1 and C2$'$(i) hold, and let $h\in\mathcal V$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] the following are equivalent:
\emph{(a)} $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}h=0$ in $L^{2}(\Pi)$;
\emph{(b)} $E\big[\widetilde W\,\{h(X_2)-h(X_1)\}\,\big|\,\Delta U,\Delta Z\big]=0$ almost surely;
\item[(ii)] if in addition A1 and A4(i) hold, \emph{(b)} is equivalent to
\emph{(c)} $E\big[h(X_2)-h(X_1)\mid\Delta U,\Delta Z,W=1\big]
=E\big[h(X_2)-h(X_1)\mid\Delta U,\Delta Z,W=0\big]$ almost surely.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{corollary}[to \cref{prp:kerchar}(i): a primitive for A1c]\label{cor:a1cprim}
Instrument completeness given the residual, together with measure separability, delivers first-order
local identification.
Suppose B1(i)--(iv), C1, C2$'$(i), A1b(ii) and A1d hold. Then A1c holds, that is,
$\ker\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}=\{0\}$.
% ARCHAEOLOGY.  A1b(i) was listed here through round 7, inherited from
% lem:nusigma(ii), and is struck.  Why it is not a hypothesis: rem:nophifree(v).
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[The Fève--Florens identification route, and how far it reaches]\label{rem:ffcompare}
\Cref{cor:a1cprim} is the transplant of \citet[Prop.~2.2]{feve2014} to the conditional-independence
design, and it is worth saying exactly what the transplant delivers and what it does not.

\emph{Notation, fixed once.} \Citet{feve2014} write the endogenous regressors as $Z_1,Z_2$ and the
instrument as $W$; in this paper the endogenous regressors are $X_1,X_2$ and $Z$ is reserved for the
exogenous controls. All quotations below are verbatim \emph{in their notation}; the translation is
$Z_t\mapsto X_t$ throughout, and no symbol inside a quotation has been altered.

\emph{What it delivers.} Their Proposition~2.2 states: ``Let $\varphi\in E$. If $(Z_1,Z_2)$ is strongly
identified by $W$ and if $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are measurably separated the function $\varphi$ is identified.''
The two primitives become A1d and A1b(ii) here, and the argument is the same in outline: completeness
removes the period difference
from inside the conditional expectation, and measurable separability then forces the direction to be
constant, which \cref{def:spaces} sets to zero because the direction lies in $\mathcal V$. This supplies
A1c with a primitive sufficient condition it did not
previously have, and it converts the draft's condition \texttt{eq-condcomppanel} at \texttt{:127--130}
from an unreconciled display into \cref{prp:kerchar}(c) --- with two corrections: the conditioning set
must include $\Delta Z$, which the draft omits, and the statement is about the linearisation, not about
the structural function.

\emph{What it does not deliver, and why.} It does not reach A1b(iii). In \citet{feve2014} the
restriction is a conditional mean and the operator is linear in $\varphi$, so injectivity of the operator
\emph{is} identification. Under conditional independence the operator equation is nonlinear in $\varphi$,
and the two statements separate. The obstruction is nameable: membership of $\mathcal V_{CI}$ is the
family $E[\widetilde W\varsigma(\Delta Y-\Delta\varphi)\mid\Delta Z]=0$ indexed by test functions of the
\emph{observed} residual at the trial value, whereas running the argument of \cref{prp:kerchar} globally
would require the strictly larger family
$E[\widetilde W\varsigma(\Delta Y-\Delta\varphi)\varkappa(\Delta U)\mid\Delta Z]=0$, indexed also by test
functions of the \emph{true} residual, about which the restriction says nothing at a trial $\varphi$. The
two families coincide at $\varphi=\vdagger$ and nowhere else, which is exactly the gap between
first-order and global identification. \Cref{prp:compact} closes off the obvious repair: because
$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is compact it is not bounded below, so A1c does not even deliver a
neighbourhood of uniqueness.

\emph{Why recording the gap is the right response, and the precedent is sharper than a difficulty claim.}
\citet{feve2014} reject the hypothesis of their own Proposition~2.2, and their stated reason is the
excess A1d reproduces exactly: ``The assumption of Proposition 2.2 is too strong because it assumes that
$E(g(Z_1,Z_2)\mid W)=0$ implies $g(Z_1,Z_2)=0$ a.s.\ for any $g$, and we only use this property for
$g(Z_1,Z_2)$ of the form $\varphi(Z_2)-\varphi(Z_1)$.'' A1d has the same shape: it quantifies over every
$\Lambda\in L^{2}(P_{X_1,X_2})$, while \cref{cor:a1cprim} consumes it only at $\Lambda=\Delta h$, a
difference. \emph{Both papers reach a completeness condition stated over a class strictly larger than the
one the argument uses, and both decline to repair it by restricting the class} --- because injectivity of
$\Lambda\mapsto E[\widetilde W\Lambda\mid\Delta U,\Delta Z]$ on differences alone is no longer a
recognisable completeness condition and has no primitive characterisation of its own.

\emph{The two asymmetries are not the same asymmetry, and the synthesis has to say so.} Theirs runs from
the assumption to its use: the hypothesis is \emph{stronger than the argument consumes}. The one recorded
in the previous paragraph runs the other way: the restriction supplies \emph{less information than the
argument needs}, the $\varsigma$ family against the $(\varsigma,\varkappa)$ family. They are opposite
inequalities and they meet at one point --- \emph{the recognisable completeness conditions available in
either design are stated over a coarser class than the design's own information}, so an assumption
calibrated to the class is too strong and the information calibrated to the class is too weak. \emph{That
is where a future improvement would have to act, in either paper}: not by strengthening the completeness
condition, but by finding a restriction on $P$ stated over exactly the class the argument uses. A1b(iii)
is accordingly kept as an assumption, with A1d recorded as the route that reaches the linearised
condition and stops there, and with its own excess named rather than hidden.
\end{remark}
